'''Garland Edward Allen III''' (February 13, 1936 – February 10, 2023) was an American [[historian of science]] and biographer at [[Washington University in St. Louis]]. His research interests lied primarily in the [[history of genetics]], [[eugenics]], and [[evolution]]. He was a longtime senior editor of the ''[[Journal of the History of Biology]]'' (1998–2006) and he won the 2017 [[Sarton Medal]] for lifetime achievement in the history of science.

==Early life and education==
Garland Edward Allen III was born on February 13, 1936, in [[Louisville, Kentucky]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://committees.missouri.edu/honorary-degrees/docs/Whos%20Who%20Missouri.pdf |title=Who's Who Missouri |website=Washington University in St.Louis |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150405174825/https://committees.missouri.edu/honorary-degrees/docs/Whos%20Who%20Missouri.pdf |archive-date=2015-04-05 |access-date=2018-09-18}}</ref> He graduated from the [[University of Louisville]] in 1957 after studying English and biology.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|author=Kleinman, Kim|title=In Memoriam: Garland E. Allen|date=April 13, 2023|website=Newsletter, History of Science Society|url=https://hssonline.org/blogpost/1987463/Newsletter?tag=Garland+E%2E+Allen}}</ref> He completed his PhD in the [[history of science]] at [[Harvard Faculty of Arts and Sciences]] in 1966 under the direction of [[Ernst Mayr]] and [[Everett Mendelsohn]] after first earning a [[Master of Arts in Teaching]] focused on English at Harvard in 1958<ref name=":0" /> and spending four years as a high school biology teacher at [[Northfield Mount Hermon School]].<ref>{{cite book|last=MacLeod|first=Roy M.|title=Science, history, and social activism: a tribute to Everett Mendelsohn|year=2002|publisher=Springer|isbn=9048159687|pages=416|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7axYHFEomgMC&pg=PA375 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|pmc=10533620 |date=2023 |last1=Maienschein |first1=Jane |author-link=Jane Maienschein |title=Garland Allen's Last Book Project |journal=Journal of the History of Biology |volume=56 |issue=2 |pages=239–250 |doi=10.1007/s10739-023-09726-8 |pmid=37552370 }}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1967 he was hired to join the faculty of [[Arts and Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis|Arts and Sciences]] at [[Washington University in St. Louis]],<ref name=":0" /> where he remained until retiring emeritus in 2014.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Maienschein |first=Jane |author-link=Jane Maienschein |last2=Richmond |first2=Marsha |author-link2=Marsha Richmond |last3=Mike |first3=Dietrich |author-link3=Michael R. Dietrich |last4=Creath |first4=Richard |author-link4=Richard Creath |last5=Beatty |first5=John |author-link5=John Beatty (philosopher) |date=June 2018 |title=History of Science Society Annual Meeting, 2017: Sarton Medal |journal=Isis |volume=109 |issue=2 |pages=351–353 |jstor=26500798}}</ref> He was recruited by [[René Descartes|Descartes]] scholar Thomas Hall, and he later organized a series of Thomas Hall Lectures at Washington University to invite other historians of biology to speak, beginning in 1978.<ref name=":0" /> He held several visiting professorships at Harvard.

He was a regular at [[Woods Hole, Massachusetts]] and became a trustee of the [[Marine Biological Laboratory]]. In 1987, he and [[Jane Maienschein]] initiated a series of history of biology seminars at the Marine Biological Laboratory that continued to run for decades.<ref name=":0" />

In 1998, Allen and Maienschein succeeded Allen's former advisor [[Everett Mendelsohn]] as the second [[Senior Editor|senior editors]] of the ''[[Journal of the History of Biology]]'', which they continued together until passing the responsibility to Paul Farber (1944–2021) in 2006.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maienschein |first=Jane |author-link=Jane Maienschein |last2=Allen |first2=Garland E. |last3=Dietrich |first3=Michael |author-link3=Michael R. Dietrich |last4=Mendelsohn |first4=Everett |author-link4=Everett Mendelsohn |last5=Richmond |first5=Marsha |author-link5=Marsha Richmond |last6=Rader |first6=Karen |date=Winter 2021 |title=In Memory of Paul Farber (1944–2021), Third Editor of the Journal of the History of Biology |journal=Journal of the History of Biology |volume=54 |issue=4 |pages=549–550 |jstor=48762664}}</ref>

Allen was awarded the 2017 [[George Sarton Medal]] of the [[History of Science Society]]; he was named as "the preeminent historian of biology today" in his award commendation.<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life and death ==
Allen was a Marxist in his personal life and wrote several articles on its influence on his thought.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> In the summer of 1965 he went to support [[Selma to Montgomery marches|civil rights marches from Selma, Alabama]] after [[Bloody Sunday (1965)|Bloody Sunday]] and in November 1969 he went to Cuba as part of the [[Venceremos Brigade]] and spent about 5 months harvesting sugar cane.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://online.ucpress.edu/abt/article-abstract/36/5/267/10323/Science-Education-and-Culture-in-Revolutionary?redirectedFrom=PDF|doi=10.2307/4444793|jstor=4444793 |last1=Allen |first1=Garland E. |title=Science, Education, and Culture in Revolutionary Cuba |journal=The American Biology Teacher |date=1974 |volume=36 |issue=5 |pages=267–291 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

He lived with his partner and husband Larry Bennet in [[St. Louis]], where they worked together on the restoration of [[Lafayette Square, St. Louis|Lafayette Square]] and ran a [[bed and breakfast]]. He had two daughters.<ref name=":0" />

Allen died of cancer on February 10, 2023, at the age of 86.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Obituary: Garland Allen, professor emeritus of biology, 86 |url=https://source.wustl.edu/2023/02/obituary-garland-allen-professor-emeritus-of-biology-86/ |website=Washington University in St. Louis |access-date=8 September 2023 |date=24 February 2023}}</ref>

== Work ==

=== Thomas Hunt Morgan ===
Allen offered the fullest treatment of the life and work of [[Thomas Hunt Morgan]], himself a Kentucky native. Allen's extensive review of Morgan presented the story of an experimentalist who staunchly avoided open political ties to science for fear of biasing the research. His discussion of the ''fly room,'' first at [[Columbia University]], then at [[California Institute of Technology]], suggests that the collaborative environment within which Morgan worked with his students, [[H.J. Muller]], [[Alfred Sturtevant]], [[Calvin Bridges]], and [[Theodosius Dobzhansky]] played an important role in establishing ''[[Drosophila melanogaster]]'' as a model organism for genetics, and launching the careers of these titans of 20th century genetics.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Reviewed Work: ''Thomas Hunt Morgan: The Man and His Science'' by Garland E. Allen|first=William|last=Coleman|journal=The American Historical Review|volume=84 |issue=5 |date=Dec 1979 |page=1494|doi=10.2307/1861696| jstor=1861696}}</ref> Allen's work contributes to the body of history chronicling the emergence of American science.

=== Eugenics ===
Allen was an international leader on the history of [[eugenics]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://source.wustl.edu/2004/05/social-problems-such-as-obesity-cant-be-solved-through-genetics-alone-warns-biologist/  |title=Social problems such as obesity can't be solved through genetics alone, warns biologist  |last=Fitzpatrick |first=Tony |date=May 4, 2004 |publisher=Washington University in St. Louis |access-date=February 3, 2017 }}</ref> His work suggests that eugenics movements were not merely localized to Germany, Britain and America, but rather that eugenics constituted an international ideological shift from [[Social Darwinism]], whereby nature would weed out people with poor heredity, to an ideology where humanity must control its own genetic stock.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Allen|first=Garland|title=Eugenics as an International Movement|year=2002|doi=10.1016/B0-08-043076-7/03396-9|journal=International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences|pages=4882–4889|isbn=9780080430768}}</ref> He suggested that with the unveiling of the human genome, we should be cautious of a new wave of the eugenics movement.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Allen|first=Garland|title=Is a New Eugenics Afoot?|journal=Science|date=October 2001|volume=294|pages=59–71|doi=10.1126/science.1066325|issue=5540|pmid=11588239|doi-access=free}}</ref>
